We all should learn to embrace fun a little bit more.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Saturday Night Live star Ashley Padilla has become a standout performer since joining Season 50 in 2024. In her second season on the show, she scored the most screen time of any cast member and went into her third season motivated to top herself. Known for her unique comedic style and impressive sketch-writing skills, the California-born actress who almost quit comedy is just having fun while making audiences laugh. However, she was also feeling guilty about one aspect of her work until she spoke to Kristen Wiig.

Currently in Season 52 on the 2026 TV schedule, SNL has always had a deep roster of very funny people who write their own comedy skits while creating and developing a variety of characters over the years. From highly memorable to not always successful, it seems as though tweaks are always being made to be stronger, sharper, and funnier. And of course, you should have fun doing so. That’s why it was surprising to hear Ashley Padilla declare to Time that she sometimes feels guilty about having fun, but that it was Kristen Wiig who convinced her that that’s nonsense. She said:

Kristen Wiig grabbed me and was like, ‘Make sure you're having fun.' And I was like, ‘Thank you.’ Because I am. And sometimes I feel guilty about that. So to hear her be like, ‘No, do that,' it's like, ‘Yay! Okay, good. Should have fun. It should be fun.'

Whether it's performing for the folks in the live audience or the viewers at home, I can’t imagine not having fun while you’re trying to give other people a good time. How can you make other people laugh when you’re not enjoying it all yourself? But I’m very reassured to learn that it sounds like Kristen Wiig gets that and encouraged the Curb Your Enthusiasm guest star to embrace it.

Knowing that it wasn’t all smooth sailing for Kristen Wiig on the NBC series makes her the perfect cast member to reassure Ashley Padilla to have fun and enjoy herself. An apparent "breakdown" actually helped the Bridesmaids star create one of her funniest sketches, but not without first worrying that she wouldn’t be able to come up with anything new three seasons into her own run. So, she knows what she's talking about.

Padilla explained that her guilt about the fun she has on the show comes from thinking that people want to hear that comedy and being a part of Saturday Night Live is very stressful. It’s a live show in front of a live audience, with constantly moving parts, changing sets and costumes, evolving revisions, and a new host every week, which sounds both nerve-wracking and exhilarating. However, it sounds like Padilla is thriving in the environment. She added:

I do think that people want to hear that it's very stressful or something, but I just — I don't think it is.

As the show’s clear MVP and screen time leader, you might think that her audition went as well as her time on SNL has, either as the centerpiece of a wild sketch or as a key support in other people’s sketches as the straight woman. However, her instincts for what’s funny weren’t as sharp when she initially tried to impress boss Lorne Michaels, who asked her for a stripped-down do-over just as herself and without hiding behind any characters. Thankfully, that did the trick, and the rest is SNL history.

Fresh off a Halloween show with host and Obsession star Inde Navarrette, and with Druski and John Mulaney scheduled for November, you can continue to watch all the fun Ashley Padilla is having on Saturdays on NBC or with a Peacock subscription.

A "continuity of core staff" is a good thing, actually

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma, Nintendo veteran of 38 years who most recently worked on the Ocarina of Time remake, says keeping staff around long-term is beneficial to the entirety of a studio – and the quality of its franchises, too.

Speaking in a new interview with GameSpot, Aonuma explains why Nintendo – and other developers overseas – aren't as likely to face waves of layoffs as Western teams might be. Heck, this year alone, we've seen many… Microsoft's plans to cut 3,200 employees at Xbox immediately spring to mind. According to the Zelda producer, though, there are benefits to retaining your staff over the years, as Nintendo does.

"I think you see a real benefit to having some very long-term-tenured staff members around who have shared the same experiences over time because every time you get to the next step, it's easier to discuss how to proceed, or if you're going to do something new," he says. With newcomers joining the studio, you want folks who know how to introduce them to long-standing processes, series, and the like that they might be less familiar with.

"When you have new staff coming in, of course you want to make sure that you're bringing everyone up with a lot of discussion, explaining how to do things, why you're doing things certain ways, as well as the language that you're using, but that takes some more time as well." This all calls for "a bit of balance," in the producer's words: "You don't want your new staff doing things by rote or without understanding the reasons; you have to invest there."

Plus, keeping old devs in the picture doesn't mean that there's never change – the Zelda series is a good example. "You do see the Zelda team change over time, but there is a continuity of core staff, certainly at least from one project to the next, so that we have that base that we can build from and bring up new staff within it. And this is something that I think Nintendo has done for a very long time, even since Miyamoto originally worked on projects like this."

In other words, there's a healthy blend of both longtime devs and fresh faces – "and it contributes to some of the sense of continuity that you do feel in games in the Zelda franchise, for example." This checks out. Recently, Aonuma also admitted that not all of the Ocarina of Time remake devs have played the N64 original, saying "it's thanks to these young people" it was made the way that it was. But, many have, too.

That's where that "balance" comes into play, I suppose, likely contributing to the new sidequests and dungeon tweaks, or the addition of Breath of the Wild's option to turn off the UI (plus, you know, the jump button), while maintaining what made the OG so great.

#3885. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#3884. FromSoft's Switch 2 exclusive, The Duskbloods, has been delayed into 2027

"We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title"

FromSoftware's The Duskbloods - a game that is best described as Bloodborne meets Sekiro meets Dark Souls, with jetpacks and dinos thrown in - has been delayed from its 2026 launch window into an unspecified time in 2027.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," says a tweet from the game's official Twitter account. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

A follow-up message continued: "During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing."

There was a suggestion previously that the title may have launched in September, but the prospective date for the unannounced release came and went without ceremony. Many consumers were uncertain whether the game would ever make its vague '2026' release window, given we've heard nothing from either publisher Nintendo or developer FromSoft since August's playtests.

Appetite for the game is ravenous, it seems: in the aforementioned closed network test, more people applied to try the game out than Elden Ring Nightreign - and that's an impressive stat, considering The Duskbloods is only launching on Switch 2.

But maybe a bit more time in the oven is a good thing for this peculiar, experimental title: the network test hasn't been without problems, as the first session ended abruptly following major connectivity issues. Though these were ironed out by the later sessions, here's hoping a full launch will be a little more stable than that.

I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

We are back. After a long sojourn to the centre of the self, I return—having completed a journey of discovery where I reflected on what I really wanted from modding GTA 5: my true desires, true capabilities, and where I want to take this whole thing as we walk, together, into the future. I speak to you now of the wisdom I have gained from my vagabond travels, behold:

I've put roving packs of hostile cougars in the game now.

The mod to put loads of cougars in Grand Theft Auto 5 is called Cougars, which is easy to remember, and it boasts "seven special cougar types" and four difficulties. Cougar time is initiated with a tap of the delete key, at which point you may choose either Catnap, Furmidable, Feral, or Catastrophe mode, which I am led to believe affects the volume of the cat hordes dispatched against you and the potency of their armaments.

Naturally, I opted for Catastrophe, kicking off a sort of pseudo-game-show opening where Franklin, Trevor, Michael, and Franklin's celebrity bodyguard were all fleeing angry litters of cats. Then we were off, with me—as Franklin—desperately dodging leaping cougars, some of them armed with heavy machine guns, some wearing body armour, some with traffic cones for reasons known only to God. Then I teleported, and the cougars followed me.

This process continued for a few minutes before I realised that, most likely, I was not going to reach my goal of a private jet waiting on the runway at Los Santos International. I performed a rare purposeful teleport to bring myself home, at which point about 56 quintillion cougars attempted to kill me. I solved this problem with an explosive micro-SMG.

When I boarded the plane, I was told I had won, and a man with a cougar for a head and a parade of dancing regular cougars behind him all congratulated me. I teleported away in the middle of their performance. It is good to be back.

#3882. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

#3881. EA's sale to Saudi-led consortium was "final nail in the coffin" for BioWare, says studio co-founder

"I'm not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck."

One of BioWare's famous doctor-founders, Greg Zeschuk, has finally spoken about the studio's closure last week, saying it's "kind of sad" and that EA's leveraged buyout by a Saudi-involved consortium "was the final nail in the coffin".

Speaking to 80 Level, Zeschuk - who founded BioWare in 1995 with fellow medical students Ray Muzyka and Augustine Yip - said he was fishing when news of the studio's closure broke. "I got like 10 texts," Zeschuk said. "I came off the river and got to my little room and opened my phone, and it's like, 'I'm so sorry to hear about BioWare.' And I'm like, 'Oh shit.'"

By the time he flew home later, he'd already apparently digested the news and missed most of the discourse around it. "I wasn't there to share in the moment," he said, "which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it.

"I'm not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck," he added. "And I think it's kind of sad. It's actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we're from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that."

Zeschuk and Muzyka retired from BioWare in 2012, the year Mass Effect 3 was released, so they've been away from the business for a considerable amount of time. They've moved on. "I've kind of gone through all the emotions long, long ago," Zeschuk explained.

BioWare did change thereafter, he seemed to accept, but as a result of a gradual change propelled naturally by people leaving and other people coming in. "I'm not going to have so much hubris to say Ray and I were the lynchpin in the chain, our departure ruined everything," he said. "It wasn't that at all. It's a slow and insidious kind of thing and again, it's the people. The people are the key."

When he heard the private acquisition of EA had gone through, that's when he feared things might be headed to a bad place. "I think it was the final nail in the coffin," he said. "I think that was the crux of it in a sense. BioWare makes these kinds of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year, and that's a better business model in some ways."

Elsewhere in the interview, Zeschuk talked a little about the origins of BioWare selling to EA in 2008 - "We had options actually" - and about personally sliding away from story-driven games towards more action-centred games like the Nioh series and Elden Ring.

Since 2017, Zeschuk has been building a beer-brewing company called Blind Enthusiasm, which apparently now employs a dozen people and ships tens of thousands of bottles of beer a year. This interview is the only one Zeschuk has given. Muzyka has so far declined to be interviewed. The third BioWare co-founder, Augustine Yip, left the company long ago, back in 1998.

The Star Trek community has sadly seen some significant losses in recent days. Near the end of October, fans paid tribute following the passing of franchise OG Walter Koenig, and they also marked the death of Patrick Stewart. Now, William Shatner -- who has paid tribute to both actors -- is weighing in with a tinge of humor. The icon made a morbid joke on the heels of Stewart and Koenig's deaths, and I'm definitely laughing so I don't cry.

Shatner addressed fans in Cleveland, Ohio amid his continued tour of Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan screenings. The fan-favorite actor then spoke to the audience about recent events and, as Cleveland.com reported, made a joke about his own mortality in the process:

I keep looking over my shoulder for the guy with the scythe.

I don't see it as insensitive, especially when this is a 95-year-old making the joke. Honestly, I think it's natural that when we see the passing of others, it reminds us of our own mortality, and I'm sure Shatner is thinking of the fact that being only one of two remaining main cast members alive from the TOS era.

William Shatner brought this up during his talk, noting that he and estranged co-star George Takei are the last men standing. Never one to miss a chance to send a jab back at Takei, he said this about whether he'll outlive the Sulu actor:

For all the jokes he made, William Shatner offered great tributes both to Walter Koenig and to his fellow Captain, Patrick Stewart. He also clarified at his latest appearance that he didn't have a close personal relationship with either, even though he co-starred with Stewart in Star Trek: Generations.

Shatner also wasn't close with Walter Koenig, despite them working together on three seasons of Star Trek and the movies. Koenig never claimed to be a big fan of his co-star, but was often quick to praise his overall talents as an actor.

The morbid joke feels like a capstone to what has been a disappointing 60th anniversary celebration of Star Trek. Yes, there's a movie in development, but that's been the same story for the past decade. There are no shows in active development, and it feels like the entire franchise is in a holding pattern while we wait to see what the next steps are.

Fortunately, we got a couple of final performances from both Walter Koenig and Patrick Stewart, thanks to Picard. Stewart, of course, was the star of the Paramount+ series, and Koenig had a cameo in the finale as the son of Chekov.

There were efforts to get William Shatner back in the modern era of Star Trek, with the co-showrunners of Strange New Worlds revealing they had a plan to bring him back as Kirk. That plan never worked out, and Shatner recently said he didn't receive an offer to return. With that, the jury is still out on how far along that plan had gotten.

CinemaBlend continues to offer condolences to the family and friends of Walter Koenig and Patrick Stewart, as they lay their loved ones to rest. Let's also wish the best of health to William Shatner, and that sense of humor that keeps him chugging across the United States.

He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3879. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

Final Fantasy 10's Blitzball was based on The Phantom Menace's Pod Racing

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy series producer Yoshinori Kitase says that Final Fantasy 10's iconic Blitzball minigame was inspired in-part by Pod Racing in Star Wars Episode 1: The Phantom Menace – so he's pleased that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took inspiration from Square Enix's series, too.

Kitase – who served as game director of Final Fantasy 10 – spoke to IGN about being "very happy" that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was so inspired by Final Fantasy because he himself was inspired by movies he enjoyed when he was young – particularly Star Wars.

"I think I like Star Wars so much that I was afraid of using anything related to [it]," Kitase says, recalling the fear that his work would become something identical to the films. He explains, "I don't think there's something from the movie that I used directly as an inspiration for my games."

However, he does admit to a couple of major inspirations, namely Biggs and Wedge – recurring names used in the series starting with Final Fantasy 6 – who are named after Luke Skywalker's wingmen during the attack on the Death Star in the original Star Wars (Biggs Darklighter and Wedge Antilles). He recalls, "I wasn't sure about the name I was going to use for those characters. And I ended up using the names of characters from Star Wars."

Another major inspiration came when Kitase was creating the fictional sport Blitzball for inclusion in the game. He recalls, "I used an idea from Star Wars Episode 1 where there's this [pod] race and the fact of using sport inside a fantasy context, I took this idea directly from Star Wars."

Frankly, I'm more impressed that he was able to be inspired by a film that released two years earlier, which is a massive reminder of how much quicker sequels to games released, and how on fire Square Enix was at that point. Kitase directed Final Fantasy 8 which released three months before The Phantom Menace, and two years later Final Fantasy 10 – inspired by The Phantom Menace – arrived on shelves.

Final Fantasy 10 leaned into the fantasy genre after devs "learned that The Lord of the Rings was in production" and thought it would be "the next big global trend."

#3876. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

It was a big night for Democrats in the US, as a "blue wave" saw the party retake control of Congress in what CNN called "a stunning blow to Trump." Among the night's big losers is former Halo composer Marty O'Donnell, whose run for Congress ended in a spectacular, crushing defeat—and then a dunk from his congressional opponent that can only be described as brutal.

O'Donnell began his political career in 2024, saying he "never wanted to be a politician" but felt compelled to do so by what he described as the deterioration of the US: "Big tech, big pharma, big media, big whatever—all trying to control big government in Washington DC."

That effort didn't work out so well—he placed fourth in the 2024 Republican primary for Nevada's third congressional district—but he tried again in 2026, this time with the support of US president Donald Trump, which O'Donnell enthusiastically welcomed despite previously calling Trump an "idiot." Well, winds and tides change.

Anyway, O'Donnell won the 2026 Republican primary, and then got in the ring with Susie Lee, the Democrat incumbent who's held the seat since 2019. It did not go well for him.

Hey, that happens sometimes—you think you got it, and then it turns out you don't actually got it at all.

But O'Donnell's Trump-toned campaign, complete with dire warnings about open borders, Marxism and the woke left, accusations of corruption leveled against Lee, embrace of the far-right commentariat, and occasional asides to remind everyone that he's absolutely not mad about being fired by Bungie, did not exactly endear him to his political opponents, or very many other people, really.

So after dismantling O'Donnell, the re-elected Lee—who seemed to largely ignore O'Donnell's rhetoric during the campaign—sent him off into the sunset with this:

#3874. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#3873. Celeste and TowerFall dev explains why both games were suddenly delisted from Xbox

"We did this to support the BDS boycott."

Celeste and TowerFall have both been delisted from Xbox suddenly earlier this week. Per a post on Bluesky, developer Maddy Thorson says this was an intentional move, with the games being removed from sale on Xbox in support of the BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which is aimed at protesting various companies linked to, or supporting, Israel's government during the genocide in Palestine.

"For those who're asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox," states Thorson in a BlueSky post. "We did this to support the BDS boycott."

In case you're unaware, Xbox's inclusion on the BDS list is due to Microsoft's partnership with Israel and its prison system, according to BDS itself. The company has provided the country use of its Azure Cloud and AI systems, which have been used consistently over the past few years in the ongoing subjugation of Palestinians. BDS has urged people to cancel their Game Pass subscriptions, boycott leading Xbox franchises - including Call of Duty and Candy Crush - and cease purchases of Microsoft gaming products. As it stands, Celeste and TowerFall are now completely unavailable for purchase within the Xbox ecosystem.

This isn't the first time we've seen developers intentionally opt out of sales on Xbox because of the BDS movement; just a few weeks ago, Big Walk developer House House released a statement noting that its game is not on Xbox because of Microsoft's ties to Israel, and we saw the developer of Tenderfoot Tactics do the same in 2025.

"We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets," noted the Australian developer at the time. "We've made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."

Microsoft has responded to the BDS boycott previously, acknowledging that it supplied AI technology to Israel's Ministry of Defense, but claims "no evidence" it's been used to "target or harm people in the conflict in Gaza". Various reports, including the one linked above, refute this claim.

Celeste and TowerFall both remain available for purchase on PlayStation, PC, and Switch.

It's an exciting time to be a fan of the MCU, as we're just a month and change away from the next upcoming Marvel movie Avengers: Doomsday hitting theaters. Anticipation is as a fever pitch, especially considering how many beloved characters are included in Doomsday's cast list. That includes Channing Tatum, who is reprising the role of Gambit after appearing in Deadpool & Wolverine (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription). Tatum recently played that role in a new ad for Dunkin', and his accent seems way more toned down.

Channing Tatum's Gambit accent was pretty wild in Deadpool 3, and there was a running joke about the other characters not being able to understand him. He claimed he wouldn't go "full cajun" for Doomsday, and he did just that in the following Dunkin' ad. In fact, I clocked every single word he said to H.E.R.B.I.E.. Check it out below:

Talk about a game changer. While the Magic Mike icon still looks incredible in the same Gambit costume, Tatum found the right balance with his accent. He's working with the same dialect, but its dialed back so that his dialogue doesn't end up lost in the next Avengers movie. Suddenly I'm even more excited to see him back as the card-throwing mutant in The Russo Brothers' crossover film.

The Avengers: Doomsday trailer briefly showed Gambit fighting Shang-Chi, but this is the first time we're hearing him speak ahead of the movie's release. He's still got the cajun swagger, but now we can actually understand the words coming out of his mouth. I assume we aren't going to get any more jokes about the accent like we did in Deadpool & Wolverine.

Fans who spent years watching the Marvel movies in order were shook when Tatum popped up as Gambit in the third Deadpool movie. He was famously attached to play the role for years, but the project sat in development hell. Originally Disney's acquisition of 20th Century Fox felt like the death knell for him playing the X-Man, but luckily that wasn't the case. I can't wait to see what he brings to the table with Doomsday, especially since his appearance presumably will be way less comedic than the Ryan Reynolds movie.

Not only will Tatum get to play Gambit again in the next Avengers movie, but he'll be appearing alongside the OG stars of the X-Men movies. Namely legends like James Marsden, Ian McKellen, Alan Cumming, Kelsey Grammer, Rebecca Romijn and the late Patrick Stewart.

Avengers: Doomsday will hit theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Whether or not Gambit survives the battle against Doctor Doom remains to be seen, but at least we'll be able to understand him this time around.

Grand Theft Auto is far from the company's only big hitter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With GTA 6 right around the corner, Rockstar Games and its owner Take-Two Interactive will be getting ready to enjoy the fruits of their labor with a massive launch, especially if current pre-order estimates are anything to go by. But GTA isn't Take-Two's only breadwinner – CEO Strauss Zelnick reckons that "we have the best collection" of IP in the games business.

Speaking in a new interview with the Wall Street Journal (below), Zelnick defends the strength of Take-Two's full library, which may be boosted by GTA, but by no means relies on it entirely.

"We have 15 franchises that have each sold at least 5 million units in an individual release," he begins. "I think we have the best collection of owned intellectual property in the video game business, and I think that's reflected in our top line, our bottom line, and our market cap."

He continues: "In addition to Grand Theft Auto, we have Red Dead Redemption, a massive title. It sold over 65 million units in the most recent release. Red Dead Online, Grand Theft Auto Online, we have NBA 2K, which is the second-biggest sports title worldwide – the biggest in North America."

In a quickfire round, Zelnick also lists the likes of Borderlands, BioShock, WWE 2K, and Civilization, as well as mobile hits such as Words with Friends and Empires & Puzzles.

Depending on your personal preferences and biases, you may or may not agree with Zelnick that Take-Two truly has the best bank of IP – others like Nintendo could certainly give the company a run for its money with the likes of Mario, Zelda, and Smash Bros., not to mention its partial ownership of Pokemon. But there's definitely no denying its strength – even with the current highest-rated game of the year, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, out today, it's hard to think of November as anything other than Rockstar's month.

With GTA 6 delays, Take-Two CEO suggests Rockstar didn't want a Cyberpunk 2077 situation: "They had to pull the title after shipping."

The STJV union says Microsoft imposed hiring freezes at Arkane that resulted in delays and additional expenses, which it then cited as reasons for shutting it down.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"After freezing hiring for 19 months, which artificially caused delays and additional cost, Microsoft now uses those same delays and additional costs as a reason to close down the studio."

France's Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo (STJV) union has accused Microsoft of sabotaging work on Marvel's Blade and then using the inevitable results to justify Arkane's closure.

The union said development of Blade "is going fine," and that the game is on par with Arkane's previous body of work, which includes the Dishonored series, Prey, Deathloop, and the sadly overlooked Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. Despite that, "workers have to face the harsh reality: our studio might get closed because, and only because, Microsoft decided to, even if that means sabotaging the game it funded."

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the union wrote. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist. Because after freezing hiring for 19 months, which artificially caused delays and additional cost, Microsoft now uses those same delays and additional costs as a reason to close down the studio."

Closing Arkane would defy "financial logic," the union claimed, as it would likely cost more money than just allowing it to finish Blade—and furthermore, it added, Arkane is profitable—"just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

"Microsoft is responsible for the situation Arkane is in today. Microsoft is responsible for the situation the workers are in today," the union said. "So Microsoft has to take full responsibility here and act accordingly."

While its "dearest wish" is to see Arkane "live on," STJV said the studio's future has to go beyond just completing Blade. And if that's not feasible and Arkane must close, it falls to Microsoft—"the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down"—to take care of the hundreds of lives it has thrown into turmoil. Given Microsoft's essentially limitless resources, the union believes the company has a moral obligation to go beyond the bare minimum required by law: "We will not allow the lives of Arkane Studios' workers to be destroyed without the company paying a fair price."

The union is not aiming low with its demands. First, "to give employees control over the decisions that shape their future" while acquisition negotiations are underway:

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Should Arkane ultimately be closed, it demands Microsoft "funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation" to ensure employees are properly compensated:

Those are big asks, but the union isn't wrong about the resources Microsoft has at its disposal: Microsoft's net income for the first quarter of FY27 was $36.6 billion. Xbox is a small contributor to that total, but it is a part of Microsoft, and that makes it Microsoft's issue to deal with.

For now, the fate of Arkane remains unresolved: The studio fell victim to the most recent round of cuts at Xbox, but a recent report indicated that it might yet find a home with a new owner. I've reached out to Xbox for comment on the STJV union's demands and will update if I receive a reply.

#3868. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#3867. Bethesda reportedly revealing The Elder Scrolls 6 next month, and we may know what its subtitle is going to be

Bethesda's hugely anticipated and long-awaited fantasy role-playing game The Elder Scrolls 6 could be revealed "as soon as next month", a new report has claimed - right in the midst of Microsoft's ongoing restructuring efforts.

Per The Verge, this new Elder Scrolls adventure carries the subtitle "Sentinel", which aligns with fan speculation, and the outlet corroborated prior reports that the game takes place within the Tamriel region of Hammerfell. The game reportedly touches on "history of the Elder Scrolls" and will "help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts".

If the game is revealed next month - presumably The Game Awards in early December is a good place for it - it would mark eight years after The Elder Scrolls 6's initial reveal trailer, and 15 years since the release of The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim. So, it's certainly been a while, though it's worth noting that The Elder Scrolls: Online has operated all through this period, to give fantasy fans something to bide their time with.

Asha Sharma, CEO of Xbox, said she'd played the game in August on a trip to the Bethesda offices, all while a giant inflatable rat and a union protest took place outside. Indeed, this reveal would take place shortly after Bethesda suffered job cuts - as did many other Microsoft-owned studios - as part of Xbox's "reset".

Xbox has been keen to keep fans optimistic of its prospects during what is undoubtedly a challenging time for the business. Yesterday, Sharma said there was "more demand than consoles available" when addressing a 14 percent dip in Xbox hardware sales. Microsoft's latest 8-K filing - a mandated finance report publicly traded companies have to file to the SEC - states in plain terms that "Xbox hardware revenue decreased 29 percent driven by lower volume of consoles sold".

Sharma has also pointed to the record performances of Minecraft and World of Warcraft: Forever's open beta, and congratulated Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 for having its "most acclaimed release in more than a decade". But Xbox's first-party release Gears of War: E-Day reportedly only sold more than 400,000 copies across Xbox and PC, following its day-one Game Pass launch. Analysts speculate that its presence on the service potentially cut into its full-cost sales.

All the while, we're seeing studios decide to not sell their game on Xbox altogether due to the company's presence on the BDS boycott list. Earlier this month, Big Walk's developers declared the game would not come to Xbox because of Microsoft's ties with Israel. And last night, both Celeste and Towerfall were removed from Xbox for the same reason.

So it's safe to say that The Elder Scrolls 6, if it is revealed next month, will arrive into a very different world than the one it poked its head into almost a decade ago. Whether it can help Xbox turn things around: that's the question.

I’m completely OK with admitting I only started watching Big Brother during Season 28. I’m a Survivor fan, and I jumped on the Big Brother bandwagon about two episodes in after I found out that my guy Rick Devens and my girl Dee Valladares were on the show. Turns out I’m not the only one. On average, Big Brother was up 8% this season over last year, and I’d be willing to bet a bunch of those newbies were Survivor fans. That didn’t stop the hate from the Big Brother core, however.

As a first season viewer, I had a very limited understanding of how this game has been played in the past, and how winners usually land the ultimate prize money. I had seen a few episodes before just from my TV work and knew the gist, but had never committed to watching a full season of the great reality competition series, so I was very much surprised by the fan response to the crossover.

From what I generally saw online, Dee and Devens played Big Brother more aggressively than most former players, latching onto and betraying alliances earlier and more frequently, and generally saying and doing whatever they needed to in order to remain in the game for as long as possible.

In short, they were kind of playing a long haul game of Survivor, only on a different series on the 2026 TV schedule. As someone who watches Jeff Probst’s show, this was familiar and exciting for me, but a lot of the regular fanbase hated it. Even some former Big Brother players were vocal about rooting against Devens and Dee. Heck, even host Julie Chen Moonves was anti-Devens for a time (though she seemingly came around).

Many fans and even alum came out of the woodwork to express anger and dismay about the Survivor cast members joining the show. This includes alum Danielle Reyes, who actually went on to join another reality show, The Traitors, after her Big Brother run. She said during the show’s run she was OK with Dee and Devens playing but certainly didn’t want either to win.

We want to see them play the game, but we don’t want them to win because that’s our kingdom.We don’t want them to come into our Big Brother house and win, when we have this inner struggle of what’s the harder show, Big Brother or Survivor? So that’s where I stand in watching these two play this game.

So, a lot of people who have been involved or watched the show for a long time were not excited about the icons getting a shot at the prize money, and even Big Brother alum Angela Murray was lumped into that.

Apparently, the creative team behind the show did not see this response coming, despite the fact Big Brother fans and alum are notoriously vocal and sometimes toxic. (To be fair, I didn't either, as I thought the Icons made the gameplay really exciting.)

Executive producer Allison Grodner actually told EW the response to having on the icons was a “surprise,” and they thought the cross-promotional connectivity between the two shows would be more positive.

That was a surprise for sure. Everyone has their tribe, right? It’s like the UCLA versus USC kind of idea. We’re all under the CBS banner and it’s all part of the same family, but there’s definitely a territorial thing that happens. And I don’t think we realized how important that would be to our alumni.

The discourse this season was particularly interesting because this isn’t the first time a Survivor player went on Big Brother. Cirie Fields also participated a few years ago. She didn’t win, but she also pulled some moves out of the Survivor playbook during her time on the air. Perhaps that’s the difference. Dee and Devens certainly had an advantage playing together, and not being able to be voted out in Week 1.

Fellow executive producer Rich Meehan also said that Big Brother is not going to bring on just any Survivor player who asks. Dee and Devens were selected specifically because the creative team thought they could hang in the game.

When we were thinking of who we wanted to bring on, it was always about who would be a great Big Brother player. So yes, they have their Survivor legacy and they’re amazing Survivor players, but we’re like, ‘Well, who’s actually gonna be good at this game and who has the personality and the ability to endure three months?

And hang they did. In fact, Rick Devens took home the winning prize, as well as $10,000 in curse money and $50,000 for being America’s Favorite House Guest – despite the haters. Just don’t ask him to choose Survivor o Big Brother over one another.

#3865. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#3864. There are currently "no other Assassin's Creed remakes actively in development", says Ubisoft

Yesterday, Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, and the publisher's comments included quite a big surprise: there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

"One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin’s Creed remake actively in development," Ubisoft said in a statement on its website. "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories."

This has come as a shock to some players because, back in 2024, Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot specifically mentioned that upcoming remakes - plural - were in active development across Ubisoft studios. "Firstly, players can be excited about some remakes, which will allow us to revisit some of the games we've created in the past and modernise them; there are worlds in some of our older Assassin's Creed games that are still extremely rich," Guillemot said.

Given the success of this year's Black Flag Resynced - which sold over 3.5 million copies and "exceeded annual expectations within its first 14 days" - it's interesting to hear Ubisoft move away from what clearly seemed a popular way of revisiting older games. But it's worth noting that although Ubisoft isn't currently working on remakes, that doesn't mean we won't get them at some point in the future.

"Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back," the company's statement continued. "That door remains open because, after all... Nothing is true, everything is permitted." That last bit, if you're unfamiliar, is a commonly-repeated motto amongst the Assassin Order.

If you're curious about what's next for the franchise, we've got a few ideas. First, there's 'Codename Invictus', which is billed as a "PvP multiplayer Assassin's Creed experience" being led by a team of For Honor veterans at Ubisoft Montreal. The title remains shrouded in mystery, and we've seen nothing of how the game will look or play yet.

Then there's Assassin's Creed Hexe, in development at Ubisoft Montreal. This game is touted as a "darker, narrative-driven" experience that appeared to be aiming for a 16th century European setting when it was announced back in 2022. It was originally believed to be targeting a 2026 release, but earlier this year, Ubisoft head of franchise Jean Guesdon explained the publisher is "taking the time to deliver on its ambitious vision, which means we'll be quiet for a little longer". Following this, a report emerged in August stating that Hexe is still at least a year away.

The Assassin's Creed series remains a pillar of Ubisoft's output, even if the publisher has been enduring a lot of change lately. Late last year, the leader of the Assassin's Creed franchise, Marc-Alexis Côté, left Ubisoft. This coincided with a reorganisation of the company and the creation of the Vantage Studios subsidiary, established by Ubisoft and Tencent, to oversee development of the French publisher's biggest franchises, which includes Assassin's Creed.

Putting a game up on Steam right now comes with some challenges. For a start, AI has made copycats much more rampant, making it even harder to stand out, and that's after you manage to slowly get approved for release thanks to a gigantic game backlog at Valve. In response to the latter, an ex-higher up at Square Enix believes the platform needs to buck up to fulfill its responsibilities.

In a post on Steam, Valve acknowledges current delays around game approvals and says it's working on ways to speed things up. "We're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days," the company says. "Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us."

Jacob Navok, former executive at Square Enix, responded to this news on Twitter. "Steam generates 3x the revenue of Roblox while Roblox has up to 1000x more games released per day than Steam," he says. "Yet Roblox games release in seconds via an automated review system and Steam takes weeks."

Steam generates 3x the revenue of Roblox while Roblox has up to 1000x more games released per day than Steam. Yet Roblox games releases in seconds via an automated review system and Steam takes weeks. The problem is not AI games increasing the number of Steam reviews. This is bullshit being sold to you. The problem is Steam is derelict of its duty. Roblox has invested billions into app review process. When you build a product your assets are uploaded into the system as you are building, so you don't get some sudden rejection at the time of release. They have spent a lot of money on R&D and AI systems that analyze and detect problematic content, and also have appeal systems. Valve takes 30% from you as a developer but has spent nothing to invest into the systems required to handle content reviews. Absolutely shameful.November 4, 2026

This definitely isn't a one-to-one comparison. Roblox projects are made in the game platform itself and it has moderation issues of its own. Automation may be efficient, but it's prone to abuse once bad actors understand what's more likely to get dinged. Also: the firehose of slop that is Roblox is not the model Valve wants to emulate, especially as it actively seeks to control its own slop infestation.

Nonetheless, the point stands that Valve could pump more resources into this aspect of the storefront. "The problem is not AI games increasing the number of Steam reviews. This is bullshit being sold to you," Navok continues. "The problem is Steam is derelict of its duty."

Releases leaning on gen AI are exacerbating existing strain on Steam's systems. The amount of games coming out was steadily increasing even before vibe coding accelerated the amount of games and outright slop getting pushed onto the conveyor belts.

That being said, the solution doesn't seem as simple as Navok makes it out to be in a reply: "Moderation is a solvable problem if they invest billions into it."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"Poor Valve, it only generates $20bn a year with 5 people working there," he quips. "The money has to be spent on so many boats they cannot afford to hire a sixth reviewer." Doubling down on the hundreds of millions that Valve cofounder Gabe Newell has spent on yachts, he adds, "Everything for gaben's navy."

More serious is his stance on Valve's resources: "It should invest into proper tooling and humans to do reviews at scale."

This looks to be what Valve is doing, as the company just said it has "spent the last several weeks working to scale our process to match" the spike in games submitted.

Navok points to Roblox's AI-assisted detection systems for mature or problematic content, but - again - the context is fundamentally different because it's one company monitoring assets it has control over, not the same sort of open market. The complexity and variance of the games under review is incomparable.

Navok also notes how much money Valve makes annually compared to the issues it's facing. "Valve takes 30% from you as a developer but has spent nothing to invest into the systems required to handle content reviews. Absolutely shameful," he concludes.

When you have small teams facing ripoffs before their game's even out, it's hard to argue that Steam has a problem. But ripoff capital Roblox isn't a convincing North Star.

Becoming Roblox appears to be the opposite of Valve's plan, so pruning or automating reviews so thoroughly that games are cleared in seconds (read: not actually reviewed) might address the quantity issue, but not the quality one many people on both sides certainly seem to care about.

Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima says he'll be dead by then, but worries AI will eventually "play a key role" in creative fields: "Getting a finished picture is not what’s fun about drawing"

#3862. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#3861. Games industry honours beloved actor Sir Patrick Stewart, as the legendary Star Trek and X-Men actor passes away

"An emperor, a captain, and an inspiration to us all."

As I'm sure you're all now already aware, legendary British actor Sir Patrick Stewart has died, aged 86. His Instagram account announced the news yesterday, saying he died at home in Los Angeles surrounded by friends and family, following "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia".

Stewart, a poised and charming actor, was probably best known for his on-screen roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, and Charles Xavier-slash-Professor X in various X-Men films. But he also enjoyed a long and celebrated career on stage.

Stewart appeared in games, too, most notably in Bethesda's fourth Elder Scrolls game, Oblivion, as Emperor Uriel Septim 7th. He effectively kicked the adventure off, narrating the game's intro with gravitas before appearing as Septim to the player in their prison cell. There, he declared he'd seen the player in his dream and proceeded to let us free.

"I️ was born 87 years ago," Stewart's opening monologue began. "For 65 years I've ruled as Tamriel's emperor. But for all these years I've never been the ruler of my own dreams. I have seen the gates of Oblivion, beyond which no waking eye may see. Behold, in darkness a doom sweeps the land. This is the 27th of Last Seed, the year of Akatosh 433. These are the closing days of the Third Era, and the final hours of my life."

Bethesda, upon hearing of Stewart's passing, posted a picture of Emperor Uriel Septim from the recent Oblivion remaster, alongside the words: "Rest in peace to Sir Patrick Stewart - an emperor, a captain, and an inspiration to us all. Our thoughts are with his loved ones."

Stewart also notably voiced the narrator in both of MercurySteam's Castlevania: Lord of Shadows games, and appeared in a number of X-Men games and Star Trek games, as well as smaller projects like Polish Holocaust game My Memory of Us. In honour of his life and work, The Star Trek Online community gathered in large numbers, arranging spaceships in long lines to mark his passing.

Messages celebrating the person Stewart was have flooded social media overnight, written by the many people he impacted during his life and long career. Long-time X-Men collaborator and Wolverine actor Hugh Jackman said: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

And Sir Ian McKellen, the Magneto actor who was considered one of Stewart's best friends, gave an overview of the many years the two had known each other, from being "ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago", to working on X-Men together. McKellen recalled cautioning Stewart about taking the lead role in Star Trek because of the effect it would have on his stage career - advice Stewart fortuitously overrode. McKellen referred to his friend as "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic".

Rest in peace, Sir Patrick Stewart. There won't be another like you.

Voters across the country opted for nearly every local ballot measure that would curb the rate of data center expansion.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Tuesday, tens of millions of Americans voted in midterm elections to deliver a sweep of generational Democratic victories in federal and state races, reflecting a leftward electoral shift that's being interpreted as a nationwide rejection of Trumpism.

But even as Republican candidates and incumbents suffered defeats in what had traditionally been considered some of the party's most entrenched strongholds, the midterms also issued a stinging rebuke to another major source of voter frustration: Data centers. At nearly every opportunity, Americans voted in favor of local ballot measures to halt, slow, or stymie the pace of data center construction in their communities.

As tracked by Data Centers on the Ballot, across the 47 local midterm elections in the American cities and townships that featured ballot measures on data center construction, voters favored restrictions on the rate of data center expansion in 38 of the 39 completed counts. Of the eight races that remain open, voters supporting additional data center restrictions are leading in all six of the races with only partial reporting. For the two remaining races, no results have yet been posted.

Here's the rundown of the types of measures voters are supporting:

At time of writing, only one ballot measure that would have introduced data center restrictions failed: In Harwood, North Dakota, voters refused an amendment to the city charter that would have required Harwood to commission an independent review before approving new data center construction or expansion.

Aside from that one exception, it's not hard to suss out why so many of those measures have passed. NBC exit polls show that 56% of yesterday's midterm voters considered AI data centers either "crucial" or "a major factor" in their choice of Congress person, with data center opponents driven by concerns of environmental toll, energy costs, noise pollution, and—one must imagine—the upward-spiraling cost of RAM.

The saga of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s move back to the UK continues because it’s being alleged that they’re having a tough time finding their forever home. At the moment, they’re reportedly living with friends, and now, it’s been alleged that their “champagne tastes” might be keeping them from growing roots for good.

So, it was recently reported that the couple and their kids are looking to move from the main house on a friend's property in the Cotswolds to property that’s on the estate. Meanwhile, according to this new report, the pair’s alleged taste for the richer things in life is causing a problem in their house hunt, as a source told Naughty But Nice:

The report claims that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are having a hard time finding the funds to buy a £10 million property. Apparently, they are set on living in a Cotswolds home because it would be closer to King Charles. However, the money needed to do that is apparently a major hurdle they need to get over, as another source claimed:

Their house hunt has effectively stalled. They haven’t found anything they both love that they can realistically afford. It’s extraordinary that a couple who talk so much about independence are once again relying on a billionaire friend to provide them with somewhere to live.

Now, all this is alleged, and we don’t know anything solid about how Markle and Prince Harry are doing financially.

It was reported earlier this summer that it cost the couple a pretty penny to use a private jet to move back to the UK. We also know there are allegedly plans for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to travel back to the United States for the holidays. When it comes to what they can and can’t afford to own home-wise, we don’t know much outside of what’s been claimed.

Apparently, they want to keep their home in Montecito, which is worth $14.5 million. If that’s true, the funds that could come from that aren’t really an option. So, their apparent desire to keep one foot in each place is a geography problem that could add to their financial issue, as one source alleged:

They want the best of both worlds, but maintaining two homes and two lifestyles costs a fortune. Buying a £10 million estate is only the beginning. Staff, security and maintenance would be enormous expenses.

Seemingly, Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have a vision of the home they want. However, it’s the finances needed to attain it that are the issue. As one source said, their problem is that they need to find “someone willing to lend them the money” to get their dream home.

Now, as this continues and we keep an eye on things like Markle and Prince Harry’s seemingly rocky deal with Netflix, it will be interesting to see if/when they finally put down roots and buy a forever home.
