Spoilers ahead for the first four episodes of Hulu's The Mob.

Over the last few years The Traitors (which is streaming with a Peacock subscription) has become one of my favorite shows of all time. The Emmy-winning reality show is showing no signs of slowing down, and the studio behind it has given us another campy competition series with The Mob. I'm having a blast watching its first season on the air, but I'm seriously mad that two of my three favorite cast members are already gone.

The Traitors cast lists are full of reality TV legends, and a solid group was also assembled for The Mob. The first two episodes proved that Willam Belli is reality TV gold, and she is a big reason why I was so invested in the show. I was also excited to see both The Sopranos star Aida Turturro and Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli in the show as well, but they unfortunately both got whacked in the 3rd and 4th episodes, respectively.

Willam is my favorite RuPaul's Drag Race queen, so I was always going to be watching The Mob with my Hulu subscription. Still, the cast announcement thrilled me thanks to seeing a bunch of other familiar faces. The fact that a Sopranos star was included seemed brilliant, and I was so ready to see what Janice herself, Aida Turturro, would bring to the table.

She might have only been in three full episodes, but the Emmy-nominated actress was wildly entertaining. Whether she was talking non-stop during the wine job or screaming for Romeo during Episode 3, I couldn't get enough. There was talk about her being voted as the new Don, which would have thrilled me. It's for this reason that I was doubly disappointed when Real Housewives of New Jersey star Joe Gorga whacked her at the top of Episode 4.

Before this heartbreak, Bruno from DWTS was similarly whacked by Joe at the top of Episode 3. Despite pledging allegiance to him as Don, Bruno's time on the show ended up being cut short. Considering what a soundbite machine he is, this feels like a real missed opportunity for the burgeoning reality competition series.

I'm watching Dancing with the Stars for the first time this season, so I was curious about how Tonioli would be different on a show like The Mob. I was surprised and delighted to see that there was basically no change in the dancer and TV personality. He was still dramatically waxing poetic, just as he does when offering critiques on DWTS. This cracked me up, which is why I was so miffed that he got eliminated.

Luckily for me, Willam Belli is still in the game, and has gotten envelopes in 3/4 of the missions so far. If she gets eliminated, I will be seriously angry, as that leaves mostly people I'm not familiar with... the exception being the truly iconic Debi Mazar.

New episodes of The Mob air Mondays on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Fingers crossed that Willam stays safe from being whacked... or even becomes the new Don. I mean, imagine the looks she'd pull out!

#3829. Activision to remove Itaewon crowd crush footage from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and apologises to victims' families

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims."

Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

In a new statement reported by Inven Global, Activision said the footage "will be completely removed" via a game update scheduled to roll out on 12th November.

The statement was issued in Korean, and the quotes come via Inven Global's AI-assisted, editor-reviewed translation.

As we reported earlier this week, the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died. The bereaved families' association and the Citizens Countermeasure Meeting called for its removal.

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims who were deeply hurt by this incident, as well as to everyone we have caused concern," Activision said.

The publisher also said that Modern Warfare 4 "is a work of fiction created to provide realistic immersion", and it "never intended to evoke or trivialise any tragic event, including the Itaewon crowd crush" by using real news broadcast footage.

The controversy has also reached the South Korean government. During a press briefing, minister of the interior and safety Yun Ho-jung described the footage's inclusion as "secondary harm", and said: "I believe appropriate sanctions should be imposed".

"Using such a tragedy as material for a game, a form of entertainment or business, is something that should be refrained from as a matter of human ethics," Yun added. He said it was up to the relevant agencies to decide "whether to impose punishment or block it to make general access difficult".

Activision's earlier statement to Eurogamer said the opening cinematic "utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative", and was "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".

#3827. Ablahshikar is a maximalist, sickos only salvage-survival CRPG about ripping organs out of warships and pawning off strange goods that's now out in early access

I don't know what's going on, and I like it

Sometimes, you come across a game and instantly know it's for the sickos. Today that is Ablahshikar, a "turn-based salvage-survival CRPG adrift on the Candle Sea" where you rip out the organs of enemy warships to "rebuild your vessel into a doomed chimera," that is out now in early access. To be honest I could have just called it a CRPG and still labelled it as a game for sickos, yet everything that's going on here is obviously just doubling down on the sick factor.

Ablahshikar is a particular flavour of maximalism. Having not played it, it feels a bit impossible describe, I mean, just have a read of some of the game's Steam page: "Lo, destiny crooks a finger only to those whose eyes peer beyond þe next tempest. Take custody of a faltering war-barge that wanders the outer brine of Dastgerd. Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." I don't know what any of that means! And I love it. Reminds me of Hylics in that the game's world is not translating itself for its audience; you take what you're given, and you figure it out yourself.

Judging from trailers and screenshots, there's a mix of activities to be getting on with. Occasionally you'll be piloting a strange, not alien, but definitely ancient ship of some kind in an arcadey sort of fashion. Then occasionally there's something that resembles Caves of Qud, i.e. some odd, 2D maybe dungeon crawling where your moves are dictated by individual keys on your keyboard. Then there's Disco Elysiumy cutscenes that feel like a video game designed in the year 1200 by someone from the year 2200, aesthetically anyway. As I said, it is a particular flavour of maximalism.

Truthfully, I do not know if I am sicko enough for Ablahshikar. Its mighty vision is terrifying, but I certainly am curious about it. Right now it's less than a fiver, and it'll only be in early access for roughly a couple of months where the price will then go up, so perhaps it's best to get in at the ground floor. If you are one such sicko, then you can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3826. PUBG live-action series in the works at Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct and star

PUBG is being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

Krafton announced the adaptation on 30th October, adding that Glover's brother Stephen, his writing partner on Atlanta, will join the project as a writer and executive producer.

The series will also be executive produced by Michael Schaefer for Neon TV, Fam Udeorji for Gilga, and Taeseok Jang and Sujin Lee for LV3H. LV3H is Krafton's entertainment arm, and it's involved in both developing and producing the show.

There's no word yet on a release window, plot, or who else will star.

Glover is a two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner, best known for Atlanta and Community. Krafton calls PUBG "one of the world’s most enduring gaming franchises", and says the game, which is credited with popularising the battle royale genre, holds seven Guinness World Records.

Earlier this month, Krafton revealed it was ending development of PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction shooter spin-off announced nearly a year ago. The publisher’s other games include Subnautica and InZoi.

#3825. BioWare are gone, but at least you'll be able to watch their final days in a documentary next year and oh wait that's really sad actually

It feels like every single week for the past few years has been the infinitely quotable 30 Rock quote on repeat. That feeling struck particularly last month when EA decided to shut down the iconic Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare. That obviously resulted in the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, of which a leaked trailer and some, now former, devs made sound pretty interesting. But hey! At least there's a documentary coming next year all about the studio that managed to capture the studio's last days! Yeah, I'm not so convinced by this upside either.

As reported by Deadline, Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie will be helming a documentary about the beloved RPG studio for Canada's Super Channel. It's called, punnily enough, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, and will apparently take a look at its origins in 1995 all the way up to its closure and a bit beyond, planned for release in 2027. Filming began two years ago, so clearly this was meant to be much more of a celebratory project than the funeral procession it's going to be.

Some big names from BioWare's history will be appearing in the doc, including its founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip, alongside the likes of longtime devs like Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone. You can also expect appearances from Jennifer Hale, Casey Hudson and, as if his sole goal is to haunt this industry everywhere, Geoff Keighley.

In a statement, co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk said, "When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and deeply moved. BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about the stories brought to life by the amazing people on our dev teams, and the fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again."

Obviously the documentary won't only be about the studio's closure, it sounds like a much bigger effort than that, so hopefully it will be a way to recognise how much of an influence BioWare has had on RPGs. It's just a ridiculous shame that it's something of a posthumous release. Continued solidarity with all those at BioWare.

Nintendo confirmed the date during yesterday's surprise Pikmin Day Direct, which also revealed that a demo will land on the Nintendo eShop on 2nd November. Any progress you make in the demo will transfer to the full game if you buy it.

Dandori Academy is a timed exam mode. The Direct showed off one of its exams, Gargantuan Garden, which challenges players to collect gold nuggets before time runs out (thanks, Insider Gaming).

Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who directed classic games such as Super Mario 64 and produced The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - recently argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent.

This is an absolutely massive day for PC Gamer writers called Joshua Wolens.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Reader, a confession: each night, before I retire to my chambers, I light a small votive candle. Bowing over it, I clasp my hands and beseech the ghost of Josh Sawyer (who is not dead) to return to the Pillars of Eternity games and add the weirdly-decent gamepad support they got on console to their PC iterations. I am an old man who wants to play them on my Steam Deck, and the existing Steam Input templates don't cut it for me.

My prayers are answered. In an announcement yesterday, Obsidian declared that now is the time of the Pillars of Eternity and Deadfire: Controller Support Public Test. Both PoE 1 and 2 have ongoing Steam betas that will allow you to play with full, start-to-finish controller support. You can opt into them and try the new feature for yourself by visiting each game's properties and opting into their respective November 4 beta versions.

Being betas, they're a touch buggy right now. Indeed, one of Obsidian's very first notices to players in the public test's announcement is "This is a public test, so please expect bugs", but I'm nevertheless impressed by the limited time I've spent mucking around with the games on Steam Deck.

There are a couple of misaligned gamepad prompts, and a very slight amount of awkwardness with the analogue movement, but frankly my main takeaway is 'Dang, it's kind of wild how well these isometric CRPGs adjust to non-keyboard-and-mouse support'. Which, yeah, is how I felt about the console versions too.

The public test runs until November 25, and the devs will use the data gathered to iron out wrinkles like those I just listed for a full release.

It's not all about gamepad support, by the way. Just, you know, mostly. Obsidian also announced patch 1.3.10.0 for PoE 1 and patch 5.1.0.0 for Deadfire. In PoE 1's case, the patch mostly smooths out some minor niggling bugs with the UI and the game's recently implemented turn-based mode.

Deadfire's patch is meatier: that game's older turn-based mode has been rejigged to integrate the improvements from PoE 1's turn-based mode. Characters no longer take a single turn per round (instead, they move as much as their initiative allows), lethality has been greatly increased—that kinda thing.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I'm a die-hard real-time-with-pause guy, so it's all fairly academic to me, but PoE 1's turn-based innovations got a lot of plaudits from players who were very hopeful they would end up ported back to Deadfire. My friends, this one is for you.

Roseanne Barr has made it clear that she hasn’t really been on speaking terms with her Roseanne co-stars since she was fired from the 2018 revival. More recently, the actress found herself engaged in a back-and-forth with one of her longtime scene partners, Michael Fishman. The viral exchange between the two sitcom veterans led to Barr dropping a total of 13 F-bombs. Now, Fishman is opening up about what his feelings on Barr are in the aftermath of the verbal skirmish.

In August, Fishman – who played D.J. Conner – opened up about receiving social media messages from users who defend Barr and join her in criticizing her collaborators for moving on to the spinoff series, The Conners, without her. Fishman said he’d historically sought to block out such comments and turn the other cheek though, this time, he expressed agreement with the claim that Barr holds racially biased views and that Roseanne was fairly canceled after her tweet about Valerie Jarrett.

Barr responded to her on-screen son’s comments during an appearance on the Can’t Be Censored, during which she argued that Fishman was a “brainwashed bigot.” While dropping expletives, the comedian also argued that Fishman exuded prejudice for not listening to the comments she’s made. Fishman later expressed his desire to move forward but, during an interview with E! News, the former child actor still expressed warm feelings towards Barr:

I loved Roseanne from the first moment I met her at the audition, and she and I bonded. And that just grew over the course of the show. I'm always going to love her. I’m always going to care about her.

Fishman and Barr originally worked together on the first nine seasons of Roseanne, which aired on ABC from 1988 to 1997 (and is available to stream with a Peacock subscription). The show then returned in 2018 for a nine-episode tenth season on the Alphabet Network, and the show had already been renewed ahead of Barr’s firing. In the aftermath, Barr heavily criticized co-star and series EP Sara Gilbert for not defending her. Fishman doesn’t agree with Barr’s views, but that doesn’t inhibit his feelings:

Look, what I'm going through in a public sense is something a lot of people are going through in the private sense, which is we all love our family members. It does not mean we agree all the time. And the truth about that is just because you don't agree, it doesn't mean you stop loving each other.

Barr recently spoke about promises that were allegedly broken after she signed off on the Roseanne spinoff. She gave the OK on the conditions that ABC execs would publicly say she was not a racist and that the crew of The Conners would know that she helped to retain their jobs. According to the She-Devil alum, “it was all a trick,” and she allegedly wasn’t given the due she was expecting.

Meanwhile, Michael Fishman has maintained a relatively low profile since being let go from The Conners (for unknown reasons) after Season 4. Fishman has still, however, continued to speak affectionately about the show’s impact, including its early LGBTQ representation. As for whether Roseanne Barr will respond to his latest comments about her, that remains to be seen.
